top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) answers a first-order question, namely who gains and loses when technology and trade shift labour demand. It pairs an explanatory framework (skill demand and supply, the education-technology race) with transparent quasi-experimental evidence on local labour markets. That pairing of new evidence and a framework that explains it is what I weigh most heavily. The core work has been replicated, extended and contested for a decade or more, and critiques have refined magnitudes and persistence without overturning the finding of slow, geographically concentrated, costly adjustment. The cost is attribution under the three-name cap: Dorn is excluded, and Katz's strand overlaps partly with Goldin's 2023 recognition. I would word the citation around labour demand, wages and regional employment, not the task model or any effect size, and I would accept Autor, Dorn and Hanson if the committee narrows the citation to import competition. P002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) has the cleanest attribution and is mature, but its quantitative importance is established more indirectly and it is adjacent to the 2022 prize, so I rank it second. A clear award is better than no award, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: No personal, co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz, Kiyotaki or Moore is apparent from the profile. I presented Goldin's 2023 prize, and Katz is a long-time Goldin co-author, which I disclose as context for the overlap, not as a tie to Katz. I am on the AER Board of Editors (2025-), and my field of labour economics is adjacent to B027. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
